treatment through micro-aeration strategy: The role of 
micro-oxygen environment

A B S T R A C T
Micro-aeration has been regarded as an efficient, economical, and promising strategy for enhancing the anaer­
obic hydrolysis acidification (HA) of toxic and recalcitrant organics. However, the available information on both 
its application in actual refractory industrial wastewater and the molecular-level interrelated mechanisms of 
functional genes and functional enzymes in pollutants degradation is limited. Herein, micro-aeration HA was 
exploited to investigate the degradation performance of actual coal gasification wastewater under various dis­
solved oxygen (DO) concentrations. In contrast, the optimal removal efficiencies of chemical oxygen demand, 
NH3–N, total organic carbon, and total phenols reached 53.3 %, 14.63 %, 56.5 % and 48.1 %, respectively, as 
well as biodegradability and detoxification capacity at 0.2–0.3 mg/L of DO. Especially, the micro-oxygen 
environment demonstrated a proclivity for the removal of phenolic compounds. And the activities of func­
tional enzymes associated with phenolic degradation (phenol hydroxylase, catechol 1,2-dioxygenase and de­
hydrogenase) were increased. Besides, organics hydrolysis-related, toxic and recalcitrant organics degradation- 
related, ring cleavage enzyme-related and facultative species under 0.2–0.3 mg/L of DO were more abundant 
than that in reactor without DO. Finally, this micro-oxygen condition also improved the abundance of genes 
expressing functional enzymes involved in the metabolic processes of phenolic biochemical degradation (e.g., 
phenol/toluene 2-monooxygenase, catechol 1,2-dioxygenase, muconate cycloisomerase). This study provides a 
theoretical basis for the industrial application of micro-aeration strategy for the detoxification pretreatment of 
refractory industrial wastewater.
1. Introduction
Refractory industrial wastewater (e.g., coal gasification wastewater 
(CGW)) originates primarily from chemical and energy sectors (Li et al., 
2023). CGW contains complex organic pollutants including phenolic 
compounds, heterocyclics, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, 
exhibiting poor biodegradability and acute biotoxicity (Ma et al., 2022). 
These characteristics not only hinder conventional treatment processes 
but also pose significant environmental and public health risks, making 
CGW management a critical challenge in advancing sustainable coal 
chemical industries (Gui et al., 2019).
Zero-emission treatment for CGW typically involves ammonia/ 
phenol recovery, biochemical treatment, advanced oxidation, mem­
brane concentration and evaporative crystallization (Ji et al., 2016). The 
anaerobic process served as a linchpin in facilitating the hydrolysis of 
substantial recalcitrant organic molecules into biodegradable fractions, 
enhancing biochemical characteristics and mitigating toxicity (Shi et al., 
2022). However, CGW toxicity severely inhibits anaerobic bacteria, 
reducing pollutant removal efficiency (Li et al., 2022b). Conventional 
anaerobic processes exhibit limited toxicity resistance and low effi­
ciency, necessitating enhanced pretreatment to optimize downstream 
aerobic treatment. While additives like diverse co-metabolic substrates

Micro-aeration, by introducing limited air or oxygen, enhanced the 
hydrolysis acidification (HA) of anaerobic system via promoting volatile 
fatty 
acids 
(VFA) 
production 
and 
wastewater 
detoxification 
(Fdz-Polanco et al., 2009). This cost-effective strategy has improved 
anaerobic HA (AHA) efficiency for toxic organics (e.g., 2,4-dinitro­
phenol, benzene, xylene, aniline, and aldehydes) in petrochemical 
(Wu et al., 2015), 2-butenal (Song et al., 2019), and resin (Dur´an et al., 
2008) production wastewater. Key evidence includes: (1) refractory 
organics removal increased from 38.7 % to 82.1 % under 0.2–0.3 mg/L 
of dissolved oxygen (DO) (Wu et al., 2015); (2) the removal efficiency of 
phenols was increased from 11.6 % (anaerobic condition) to 80.7 % 
(micro-oxygen condition, DO: 0.41 mg/L) (Yang et al., 2018); (3) 
micro-oxygen also enhanced biodegradability of chemical industrial 
park wastewater as biological oxygen demand/chemical oxygen de­
mand (B/C) ratio rose from 0.46 to 0.61 after 48 h hydrolysis with 
carriers at filling ratio of 30 % (An et al., 2020). It also alleviated 
ammonia nitrogen (NH3–N) inhibition in the anaerobic expanded 
granular sludge bed (Haroun et al., 2025). However, current research on 
micro-aeration in refractory wastewater treatment remains limited to 
specific industrial streams, with insufficient systematic analysis of oxy­
gen dosage thresholds, process synergies, and long-term stability that 
critical gaps hinder its industrial scalability. Moreover, there is no sys­
tematic understanding of microbial ecology (e.g., microbial activity, 
variations of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS)) during actual 
industrial wastewater treatment under micro-oxygen environment.
The facilitative mechanisms of micro-oxygen encompassed the 
incorporation of oxygen in the ring-opening reactions of cyclic organic 
compounds, the amplification of enzymatic activity, and the prolifera­
tion of functionally specialized microbial communities (Zhang et al., 
2021). Although existing studies have focused on microbial community, 
the molecular genetic and physiological functionality of microbes that 
enhance the degradation of refractory organics remain significantly 
understudied. Aromatic organic compounds presented a formidable 
challenge to anaerobic microbial degradation, with ring-opening re­
actions constituting a critical rate-limiting step (Mu et al., 2022). 
Traditional activation of ring-opening was sluggish and typically facil­
itated by iron reduction (Nzila, 2018). In contrast, micro-aeration 
expedited this activation by incorporating oxygen molecular into the 
benzene ring via oxygenase, thereby attenuating the stability of the C–C 
bonds and rendering the organic compounds more susceptible to mi­
crobial cleavage (Fuchs, 2008; Varjani and Upasani, 2017; Zhang et al., 
2021). Enzymatic agents such as monooxygenases facilitated the inser­
tion of molecular oxygen into monoaromatic hydrocarbons, converting 
them to phenols, which subsequently underwent further ring-opening 
reactions in the presence of phenol hydroxylases or oxygenase 
(Gullotto et al., 2008). Moreover, the micro-oxygen environment was 
propitious for the amplification of enzymatic activities germane to or­
ganics degradation, particularly extracellular functional hydrolases 
(amylase, protease, cellulase, and oxygenase, etc.) secreted by faculta­
tive anaerobic bacteria (Charles et al., 2009; Lim et al., 2014). 
Micro-aeration enhanced the relative abundance of facultative bacteria. 
Notably, the phylum Firmicutes exhibited a marked increase in relative 
abundance, particularly within Longilinea and Clostridium, resulting in a 
threefold surge in the concentrations of acetic and butyric acids (Song 
et al., 2019). This phenomenon has been verified across a range of 
simulated wastewater studies (Zhang et al., 2022). Consequently, the 
more detailed examination of microbial species, functional genes, and 
metabolic pathways would be instrumental in elucidating the mecha­
nistic basis and performance attributes of micro-oxygen, thereby 
fostering its practical implementation and broader adoption in future 
applications (Bovio et al., 2019).
Herein, the bench-scale UASB reactors with various aeration condi­
tions (0, 0–0.1 and 0.2–0.3 mg/L of DO) were designed for the HA 
treatment process of CGW in this study. Then, the removal performance 
of different pollutants, the biodegradability and biotoxicity of CGW

the transform of dissolved organic matter (DOM) under the anaerobic 
and micro-oxygen environments was analyzed in detail. Subsequently, 
microbial activity, functional enzyme activity and EPS variation were 
tested to explore the effect of micro-oxygen environment on microbes in

enhanced HA for actual CGW treatment through microbial community 
structure, functional gene abundance, and metabolic pathways of 
representative pollutant (phenol).
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Characteristics of wastewater and inoculum
The actual CGW biological treatment process influent was the 
effluent after the ammonia/phenol recovery process, and the main 
purpose of this study was to improve the effect of biological treatment. 
Therefore, the CGW utilized in this study was sourced from the waste­
water treatment plant (WWTP) of Henan Yima Coal-to-Gas Co., Ltd, 
China, having undergone pretreatments via ammonia stripping and 
phenolic solvent extraction. Exhibiting dark brown in color with pro­
nounced chromacity, the CGW carried strong aromas of coal tar, as 
depicted in Fig. S1(a). Detailed water quality matrix is provided in 
Table S1 with COD, BOD, NH3–N, total nitrogen (TN), and total organic 
carbon (TOC) values of 3317 mg/L, 1200 mg/L, 263.2 mg/L, 315.4 mg/ 
L, and 1247 mg/L, respectively. To simulate and reveal the actual 
biochemical treatment process, the influent remained devoid of any 
additional inorganic elements, nutrients or co-substrate carbon sources. 
The inoculation sludge, procured from the anaerobic tank of the above 
WWTP, manifested black color and lacked optimal flocculation, as 
illustrated in Fig. S1(b). The concentrations of mixed liquor suspended 
solids (MLSS) and mixed liquor volatile suspended solids (MLVSS) stood 
at 6.5 g/L and 5.3 g/L, respectively, yielding the MLVSS/MLSS ratio of 
~0.82. The associated sludge volume index was 105, indicative of its 
excellent settling capacity.
2.2. Batch experiments
Micro-aeration hydrolysis acidification (MAHA) batch experiments 
were performed in blue-capped bottles, in which 150 mL of CGW and 50 
mL of sludge with supernatant discarded by centrifugation were added 
firstly. Anaerobic control group was purged with N2 for 15 min and the 
complete removal of DO was verified by litmus blue test paper, then the 
rubber cover was immediately tightened. The operation of micro- 
aeration experiment was directly exposed to the air. Then the bottles 
were placed in a thermostatic shaker (35 ◦C), and reacted at 150 rpm for 
74.5 h. During the experiment, DO and oxidation–reduction potential 
(ORP) levels were monitored using a DO sensor (MIK-DY2900 meter, 
Asmik, China) and an ORP instrument (HQ30d, Hach, USA), respec­
tively. And the DO and ORP values were controlled at 0.27 ± 0.06 mg/L 
and −273~−294 mV, respectively, thereby satisfying the micro-oxygen 
conditions. Water samples were taken at the given intervals (0, 13, 26.5, 
40.5, 50.5, 67 and 74.5 h) and filtered through the membrane (0.45 μm) 
for the detection of COD, TOC, NH3–N and Tph concentrations. Long- 
term batch mode of CGW degradation performance under aerobic and 
different DO conditions is described in the Text S1, Supporting 
Information.
2.3. Bioreactor set-up and operation
The anaerobic HA reactor employed in this study was the UASB 
reactor, featuring an internal diameter of 30 mm, a height of 900 mm, 
and an effective volume of 0.5 L. CGW was introduced into UASB 
through the lower inlet via a peristaltic pump, subsequent to DO elim­
ination via N2 aeration. The effluent was subsequently channeled from 
the apex of reactor into a collection reservoir, following sedimentation 
within a reflux tank. Sludge settled at the base of tank was recirculated 
into the UASB through a reflux pump, operating at a regulated reflux 
ratio of 1:6, thereby ensuring homogenous sludge suspension within the 
reactor at an upward flow rate of 0.55 m/h. Thermal stability within the 
reactor was maintained at 35 ◦C via a water bath, and the reactor 
structure and flow path are delineated in Fig. 1 and Fig. S2.
In this study, three parallel UASB groups (HA, MAHA-1 and MAHA- 
2) were established. The HA reactor served as the anaerobic HA control 
group, while MAHA-1 and MAHA-2 reactors functioned as the micro- 
aeration HA test groups, with DO concentrations meticulously regu­
lated at 0–0.1 mg/L and 0.2–0.3 mg/L, respectively. The reactors 
employed the microporous aerator (with an aperture of 5 μm) situated at 
its base, connected to an aeration pump, to establish a micro-oxygen 
environment. This setup was accurately regulated using DO sensor and 
ORP instrument, while inspections and recordings were carried out at 
3–4 h intervals. Given the expansive diameter of the UASB and the rapid 
upward sludge flow rate, elevated aeration levels were eschewed to 
mitigate foam production and potential sludge loss, thus precluding the 
establishment of higher DO concentration in this investigation.
The initial sludge concentration was set at 6 g/L for all reactors, and 
the hydraulic retention time (HRT) was calibrated at 36 h. Due to the 
high toxicity of CGW, the influent concentration was incrementally 
escalated until stabilization was achieved, over a total operational 
period of 90 d Reactor operation stages and conditions are shown in 
Table S2. Water samples were subjected to membrane (0.45 μm) filtra­
tion for the assessment of general indicators, while the obtained samples 
during the stable stage underwent comprehensive analysis for 
biochemical attributes, toxicity levels, and organic compound charac­
teristics. Notably, during sample collection, immediate adjustments to 
the valve of aeration pump were executed whenever DO and ORP 
deviated from the set values.

To obtain the composition and characteristics of DOM in CGW, the 
excitation-emission-matrix (EEM) was measured by a fluorescence 
spectrophotometer (F-7000, Hitachi, Japan), and the specific operation 
steps were according to the previous study (Xiao et al., 2016). EEM data 
was further analyzed by the regional fluorescence integral method. 
Mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) and different fluorescence ratios 
(HIXsyn, BIX, FI, HIXem and PeakT/C) were used to characterize the 
fluorescence properties of organics in water samples according to the 
description of (Xin et al., 2020). Where, MFI refers to the total fluores­
cence intensity per unit of TOC, BIX and FI represent the contribution of 
biologically produced organics, and HIX and PeakT/C are the humifi­
cation index and biochemical properties, respectively. The parallel 
factor method (PARAFAC), based on the principle of trilinear decom­
position theory and alternating least squares, can identify the charac­
teristic components more clearly than the traditional method of EEM 
data analysis (Sciscenko et al., 2022). Therefore, the PARAFAC method 
was further used in this study to investigate the removal of major fluo­
rescent organics from CGW.
2.4.2. Cytotoxicity and specific toxicity tests
Photobacterium luminescens T3 (Beijing Haifuda Technology Co., 
China) was selected as the test organism for the toxicity analysis of 
samples, and the toxicity test was carried out according to GB/T 
15,441–1995 (China) (Kurvet et al., 2011). The median effect concen­
tration (EC50) was calculated by testing the inhibition rate of water 
samples at different dilution gradients, then the variation of toxic unit 
(TU) value of was calculated according to EC50 (Eq. (1)).

2.4.3. Microbes activity analysis
The detailed analytical procedure for the live/dead cells of sludge is 
provided in Text S4, Supporting Information. The adenosine triphos­
phate (ATP) content of sludge was utilized to characterize the sludge 
activity at different DO concentrations. The sludge (0.5 mL) was washed 
three times with 0.1 M phosphate buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.2–7.4) and 
analyzed by Promega ATP kit. The degradation activity of sludge for 
organics can be obtained from the dehydrogenase (DHA) activity. 
Sludge washed with PBS was tested using Mibio Soil Dehydrogenase Kit 
(96T). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, PP3010T, Quorum, UK) was 
applied to observe the surface damage of cell. The sludge sample (0.1 
mL) was first diluted 100 times and then filtered through the membrane 
(0.45 μm). The sludge left on the membrane surface was fixed by 
glutaraldehyde solution and washed with PBS, followed by dehydration 
with 50 %, 70 %, 80 %, 90 % and 100 % ethanol and isoamyl acetate for 
10 min, and the critical point was dried for 2 h and the surface was 
sprayed with gold for measurement. The specific detection methods for 
phenol hydroxylase and catechol dioxygenase are provided in Text S5 
and Text S6, Supporting Information, respectively.
2.4.4. EPS extraction and analysis
Thermal extraction was employed to extract EPS from activated 
sludge. The sludge mixture was washed three times with ultrapure water 
and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was firstly 
filtered through membrane (0.7 μm), and the remaining sediment was 
diluted to its original volume with NaCl solution (0.05 %, 50 ◦C) and 
then shaken for 1 min and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 5 min. The su­
pernatant was further filtered through a membrane to obtain loosely 
bound EPS (LB-EPS). The remaining sediment was again diluted to the 
original volume with NaCl (0.05 %), centrifuged for 5 min at 4000 rpm 
after a water bath at 60 ◦C for 30 min, and the supernatant obtained by 
filtration was tightly bound EPS (TB-EPS). Phenol-sulfuric acid method 
was employed to determine the polysaccharide content of LB-EPS and 
TB-EPS, while protein and humic acid were determined by the modified 
Lowry method (Zhang et al., 2022). Besides, EEM spectra were further 
analyzed for LB-EPS and TB-EPS, and the data obtained was processed in 
conjunction with the PARAFAC technique.
2.4.5. Microbial community and genetic analysis
The detailed description about the operation of microbial commu­
nity and genetic analysis, including statistical method is shown in Text 
S7, Supporting Information.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of bioreactors under different DO concentrations
To ascertain the role of micro-aeration in the HA process of CGW, 
initial batch experiments were employed to juxtapose the impact of 
MAHA against anaerobic HA. The anaerobic process exhibits a lag 
period of ~26 h, during which the concentrations of COD, TOC, NH3–N, 
and Tph exhibit a marked decline until 40 h (Fig. S3). Phenolic com­
pounds, particularly polyphenols such as catechol, which are abundant 
in CGW, exerted pronounced acute toxicity to microbes, conceivably 
accounting for the protracted lag period in the anaerobic reaction (Kim 
et al., 2008). Conversely, MAHA exhibits no discernible lag period, 
signifying that the presence of DO mitigated the wastewater toxicity, 
thereby abbreviating the lag period of anaerobic process. Anaerobic HA 
facilitates the removal of 65.6 %, 67.8 %, 17.1 %, and 54.7 % of COD, 
TOC, NH3–N, and Tph from CGW, respectively within 74.5 h, while 
MAHA augments the removal efficiencies of these parameters by 8.6 %, 
6.1 %, 4.7 %, and 15.3 %, respectively. Evidently, micro-aeration en­
genders a substantial enhancement in the removal of COD and Tph 
through HA process, with Tph removal being particularly noteworthy.
The COD removal efficiency of anaerobic sludge in CGW was also 
investigated at different DO concentrations (Fig. S4(a)). The results 
reveal that COD removal efficiency improves from 39.6 % to 59.2 % as 
the DO concentration increases from 0–0.1 mg/L to 0.8–1 mg/L within

The effect of USAB on the removal of pollutants from CGW under 
different DO conditions was further investigated. In Stage I (1–37 d), all 
reactors received influent that was diluted and possessed lower con­
centrations (COD: 1120–1470 mg/L). The effluent concentrations of 
COD, TOC, NH3–N, and Tph are ~50 %, ~30 %, ~50 % and ~45 %,

centration was promptly elevated. This results in the effluent 
concentration of MAHA-2 gradually descending below that of HA and 
MAHA-1 reactors, whereas the operation results of HA and MAHA-1 
reactors remain similar. This elucidates that the HA process of MAHA- 
2 is superior in environments with elevated DO levels during the esca­
lation of influent concentration. In Stage III (52–90 d), the influent 
comprises raw CGW, resulting in gradual differences in pollutant 
removal among different reactors before stabilization. It is worth noting 
that the average removal efficiencies of COD, NH3–N, TOC, and Tph by 
MAHA-2 stand at 53.3 %, 14.63 %, 56.5 %, and 48.1 %, respectively. 
Furthermore, the removal efficiencies of COD, TOC, and Tph by MAHA- 
1 and MAHA-2 surpass those achieved by HA, with MAHA-2 out­
performing HA reactor by 14.9 %, 15.5 %, and 24.0 %, respectively. In 
contrast, the enhancement of Tph removal is most pronounced under 
micro-oxygen environment. NH3–N removal efficiency through HA 
reactor (10.14 %) is relatively low, while MAHA-1 and MAHA-2 
improve it by 1.65 % and 4.49 %, respectively. Nitrogen balance anal­
ysis during Stage III reveals that the DON concentration in CGW is 39.32

Fig. S5 lists the DO, ORP and pH values during the daily monitoring 
of reactor operations. DO levels in MAHA-1 and MAHA-2 exhibit oscil­
lations within 0–0.1 mg/L and 0.2–0.3 mg/L, respectively, while HA

mV, whereas MAHA-1 and MAHA-2 maintain ORP values within

attributed to the enhanced HA process, which generates a greater vol­

Refractory organics underwent an initial hydrolysis, resulting in the 
generation of intermediates and molecular organics through ring- 
opening and chain-breaking mechanisms (Chen et al., 2023, 2020). 
Subsequently, small-molecule VFAs were produced through the activ­
ities of fermentation bacteria. During the transportation and preserva­
tion of CGW, there was a possibility of partial AHA occurring, thereby 
resulting in markedly higher concentrations of VFAs (acetic acid, pro­

3.3. Assessment of microbial metabolism and activity
3.3.1. Live/dead percentage
Live/dead cells of the sludge in the reactor were observed through 
staining with live/dead cells staining agents under laser scanning 
confocal microscope. Major dead cells are presented in HA and MAHA-1 
samples, whereas more live cells can be observed in the MAHA-2 image 
(Fig. 6(a-c)). Subsequently, the fluorescence ratio of live/dead cells was 
analyzed by ImageJ, and the live cells proportions of sludge in HA, 
MAHA-1 and MAHA-2 reactors are 28.96 %, 31.89 % and 49.32 %, 
respectively. This demonstrated that MAHA-2 mitigated wastewater 
toxicity due to the judiciously calibrated DO concentration, resulting in 
the enhanced number of live cells in the sludge and augmenting mi­
crobial activity. The microbial cell morphology in the reactor was 
further visualized by SEM. Notably, higher biotoxicity could cause 
oxidative damage to cytomembrane, resulting in microbial cell rupture 
(Zheng et al., 2018). It shows that cells in all reactors suffer varying 
degrees of rupture, with MAHA-2 exhibiting the least damage and 
thereby signifying comparatively reduced wastewater toxicity to cells 
(Fig. 6(d-f)).

3.3.3. Variation of EPS
The predominant component of EPS is protein in all reactors (Fig. 7
(a, b)). Notably, there is a marked escalation in the EPS concentration of 
Stage III (the sum of polysaccharides, proteins, and humic acids) 
compared to Stage I. This may be attributed to active secretion or passive 
release by microbes, where active secretion refers to microbes actively 
synthesizing EPS to form a physical barrier or chelating toxic substances 
by up-regulating the relevant genes under the pressure of toxic sub­
stances or C/N imbalance (Tao et al., 2025), and passive release refers to 
the release of intracellular substances due to damage to the cell mem­

et al., 2021). EPS consists of soluble EPS (S-EPS), LB-EPS and TB-EPS, of

metabolism and the release of intracellular substances after cellular 
senescence and death (Yang et al., 2022), while LB-EPS and TB-EPS are 
secreted by microbes, partly from cellular adsorption and organic 
transformation (Wu et al., 2020). Meanwhile, the contents of LB-EPS and 
TB-EPS including polysaccharides, proteins and humic acids therein are 
significantly higher in MAHA-2 at Stage III than in other reactors. 
Combined with the results of live/dead cells, MAHA-2 has a significantly 
higher proportion of live cells at Stage III than other reactors. It is 
confirmed that although increased wastewater concentration and 
toxicity accelerates cell death to release part of the EPS, and that the EPS 
may be derived from cellular adsorption and organic transformation, the 
microbial stress secretion mechanism of “active barrier” is dominant at 
Stage III in MAHA-2.

LB-EPS. This discrepancy arose from the fact that LB-EPS was porous, 
displaying a greater correlation with suspended or colloidal organics in

to environmental fluctuations, rendering it unstable. Remarkably, the 
composition and concentration of LB-EPS and TB-EPS in MAHA-1 aligns 
closely with that in HA. However, with a further elevation in DO con­

concentrations, particularly in term of protein concentration.

3.4. Microbial community analysis
The microbial community of reactors was revealed using the Illu­
mina MiSeq high-throughput sequencing method. Based on the Shannon 
dilution curve at the genus level, it can be observed that the curves of all 
sample gradually flatten (Fig. S11), indicating that the sequencing data 
sufficiently represent the entire community. Table S5 presents the 
community abundance and alpha diversity indices for each sample. The 
coverage indices are all above 0.995, indicating that the sequence 
analysis adequately represents the complete microbial community 
(Uludag-Demirer et al., 2025). The Ace and Chao indices serve to eval­
uate the total species count, indicating species richness, with higher 
value clearly signifying an increase in species richness (Jena et al., 
2016). The Shannon index integrates species richness and evenness, 
with higher value denoting an increase in diversity (Wu et al., 2023; Zou 
et al., 2020). Besides, the Simpson reflects the community dominance, 
applied as a measure of community diversity, which represents a com­
bination of species richness and evenness in a given ecosystem. When 
few dominant species are extremely prominent in the system, Simpson 
value increases and diversity decreases. Conversely, when the distribu­
tion of species is balanced, Simpson value declines and diversity rises 
(Jiang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2024). The Shannon, ACE, and Chao 
indices of MAHA-2 are higher than those of HA and MAHA-1 reactors. It 
shows that the richness and diversity of microbes in the reactor are 
higher at DO of 0.2–0.3 mg/L. The Rank-Abundance curve also supports 
this conclusion (Fig. S12). Additionally, the Simpson index of MAHA-2 is 
lower than that of MAHA-1 and HA reactors, indicating the increase in 
microbial community diversity due to the elevated DO. This not only 
enhanced microbial ecological stability but also strengthened the ability 
to withstand high-toxicity environmental pressures from CGW. It is also 
one of the reasons for the superior pollutant removal capability of 
MAHA-2.
In the microbial community at the phylum level, Proteobacteria, 
Firmicutes, Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, Desulfobacterota, Chloroflexi 
and Synergistota emerge as the dominant phyla across all reactors (Fig. 8
(a)). The key distinction between microbial phyla in anaerobic and 
micro-aeration reactors lies in their relative abundances. The relative 
abundances of microbial phyla in MAHA-1 and HA reactors exhibit a 
resemblance, signifying that lower DO concentration has limited impact 
on the microbial ecology of anaerobic system. However, as DO con­
centration increases, significant shifts occur in the relative abundances 
of dominant phyla. The relative abundances of Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, 
Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, Desulfobacterota, Chloroflexi, and Syn­
ergistota are 53.32 %, 17.48 %, 5.69 %, 3.88 %, 6.24 %, 0.72 % and 1.58 
%, respectively, in HA reactor. In contrast, MAHA-2 exhibits relative 
abundances of 45.62 %, 20.70 %, 7.36 %, 5.65 %, 1.45 %, 2.80 % and 
2.93 % for the same phyla. Notably, Firmicutes, Actinobacteriota, Bac­
teroidota, Chloroflexi, and Synergistota exhibit higher relative abundances 
in MAHA-2. Among them, Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and Chloroflexi were 
crucial phyla involved in the hydrolysis of organics by producing 
extracellular hydrolases to hydrolyze complex organics to VFAs (Bovio 
et al., 2019; Song et al., 2019).
Proteobacteria, predominantly facultative or obligate anaerobes in 
wastewater treatment systems, mostly consist of heterotrophic bacteria 
that play a crucial role in COD removal, denitrification and desulfur­
ization processes (Liu et al., 2022). However, the relative abundances of 
Proteobacteria and Desulfobacterota in MAHA-2 have decreased by 7.71 
% and 4.79 %, respectively. The micro-oxygen environment might 
inhibit the growth of obligate anaerobes, leading to a decline in the 
relative abundance of Proteobacteria. Desulfobacterota, associated with 
sulfur cycling, primarily encompassed sulfate-reducing bacteria (Song 
et al., 2021). The micro-oxygen condition could inhibit the growth of 
sulfate-reducing bacteria, resulting in a decrease in the relative abun­
dance (Zhang et al., 2021). Therefore, at the phylum level, higher DO 
concentration promoted the enrichment of phyla associated with the HA 
of organics, thereby facilitating the biodegradation of organics in 
wastewater.
The differences in the functional microbial community at the genus 
level under different DO concentrations were further explored. Ottowia 
(7.96 %), Trichococcus (6.33 %), Soehngenia (3.69 %), Lentimicrobium 
(4.76 %) and Desulfobulbus (5.44 %) are the genera with the highest 
relative abundances in the HA reactor (Fig. 8(b)). Ottowia, one of 
facultative anaerobes, could participate directly in denitrification using 
aromatic compounds as electron donors (Huang et al., 2024). Organic 
pollutants in CGW are mainly dominated by phenols, thus Ottowia has 
the highest relative abundance and plays a key role in organics degra­
dation. Trichococcus and Soehngenia are also facultative anaerobes, 
belonging to the phylum Firmicutes, which are primarily associated with 
the organics hydrolysis for acid production (Grouzdev Denis et al., 2019; 
Ji et al., 2020; Zuo et al., 2023). For instance, they could hydrolyze and 
ferment glucose, sucrose and lactose to produce various VFAs (e.g., 
lactic acid, acetate, formate, and other acids).
Lentimicrobium and Desulfobulbus are strict anaerobes belonging to 
the phyla Bacteroidota and Desulfobacterota, respectively (Sun et al., 
2016; Suzuki et al., 2007). Lentimicrobium is associated with anaerobic 
fermentation of organics (Zhen et al., 2023), while Desulfobulbus is a 
typical sulfate-reducing bacterium that reduces sulfate in wastewater to 
produce toxic H2S (Tian et al., 2017). Compared with HA reactor, there 
is little change in the relative abundance of the aforementioned five 
major microbial genera in MAHA-1 reactor. However, Ottowia, Tricho­
coccus, and Soehngenia have increased relative abundances to 11.69 %, 
7.94 %, and 5.50 % respectively in MAHA-2. Lentimicrobium and 
Desulfobulbus are inhibited by higher DO concentration, with a conse­
quent decrease in relative abundance from 4.76 % and 5.44 % to 1.20 % 
and 0.67 %, respectively. Micro-oxygen environment significantly sup­

Monferr´an et al., 2005; Verma et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016), have 
increased their abundances from 0.19 %, 1.35 %, 0.92 %, and 0.27 % to 
1.40 %, 2.52 %, 1.73 %, and 1.27 %, respectively. As a result that the 
hydrolysis rate of long-chain alkanes under micro-oxygen condition is 
faster. For example, Pseudomonas degraded n-alkanes (C11-C21) at a 
faster rate and produced more acetate (Rocha et al., 2011). Furthermore, 
genera such as Acinetobacter, Rhodococcus and Thauera, associated with 
the degradation of phenols or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (Ma 
et al., 2023; Mao et al., 2010; Szilveszter et al., 2023), have also shown 
increased abundance. In conclusion, the reactor with higher DO con­
centration has enriched genera associated with the fermentation for acid 
production, as well as the degradation of phenols, polycyclic aromatic 
hydrocarbons, and long-chain alkanes. And this enrichment facilitated 
the HA and ultimate degradation of recalcitrant organics. The evidence 
highlights the crucial role of micro-oxygen environment in enhancing 
the organics removal in actual CGW treatment.
3.5. Macrogenomics analysis
3.5.1. The links between microbial metagenomes and aromatic metabolic 
profile
Aromatic compounds have conjugated ring structure and the delo­
calization property of π orbitals, rendering the benzene rings excep­
tionally stable and resistant to microbial ring-opening cleavage (Nzila, 
2018). Thus, the ring-opening cleavage of benzene structures represents 
a pivotal rate-limiting step in the degradation of aromatic organic 
compounds by anaerobes (Boll et al., 2002). Simultaneously, it is a 
critical facet for reducing the toxicity of aromatic organics and 
enhancing wastewater biodegradability (Kuroda et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 
2018). Under the strict anaerobic condition, the system lacked 
ring-opening activators (ring-opening enzymes substrates) and terminal 
electron acceptors (e.g., O2, NO3ˉ-N, sulfate, Fe3+, and high-valence Mn) 
(Chen et al., 2023; van Leeuwen et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025). This 
circumstance forced microbes to engage in ring-opening through slower 
and lower-capacity reduction pathways, such as the methane reduction 
pathway. Conversely, O2 acted as the activator of benzene ring-opening 
reaction through the action of various monooxygenases or dioxygenases 
in the micro-oxygen environment (Zhang et al., 2021). This process 
weakened the stability of C–C bonds in the benzene rings, making them 
more susceptible to cleavage and gradual transformation into small 
molecules that were readily utilized by microbes (Zhang et al., 2022). In 
both anaerobic and micro-oxygen conditions, a variety of ring-opening 
functional enzymes and related microbes played pivotal roles in the 
auto-catalytic process (Zhu et al., 2023).
The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database 
was utilized to screen and analyze the metagenome of microbial com­
munity, and the links between dominant microbial species (>0.5 %) and 
ring-opening cleavage enzymes were constructed (Fig. S13). As depicted 
in Fig. 9(a), the ring-cleavage enzyme was listed with related dominant 
species. Under the presence of DO, aromatic organic compounds in CGW 
primarily underwent eight distinct ring-opening degradation pathways. 
The pivotal ring-opening cleavage enzymes involved catechol 1,2-diox­
ygenase, catechol 2,3-dioxygenase, gentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, proto­
catechuate 3,4-dioxygenase, homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, 3,4- 
dihydroxyphenylacetate 2,3-dioxygenase, 2,3-dihydroxyphenylpropi 
onate 1,2-dioxygenase and biphenyl-2,3-diol 1,2-dioxygenase. A total of 
15 microbial species were found to be associated with the expression of 
the above gene-encoding ring-opening cleavage enzymes (Boll et al., 
2002; Nzila, 2018). Among them, the catechol 1,2-dioxygenase, cate­
chol 2,3-dioxygenase, protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase, and gentisate 
1,2-dioxygenase possessed relatively abundant species, suggesting that 
they played the central role in the micro-oxygen ring-opening cleavage 
of aromatic organic compounds. Conversely, under anaerobic condition, 
aromatic organic compounds underwent ring-opening cleavage through 
2-ketocyclohexanecarboxyl-CoA hydrolase, benzoyl-CoA-dihydrodiol 
lyase, and 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoyl-CoA hydrolase. It’s evident that 
the number of microbial species involved in encoding is significantly 
lower than micro-oxygen condition. Notably, the microbial species are 
closely related to 2-ketocyclohexanecarboxyl-CoA hydrolase, indicating 
a greater involvement of this enzyme in the anaerobic ring-opening 
cleavage pathway. Fig. S14 shows the detailed metabolic pathways 
and specific information regarding ring-opening enzymes. Therefore, 
under micro-oxygen conditions, both the number of microbial species 
associated with ring-opening enzymes and ring-opening metabolic 
pathways are far greater than anaerobic condition. Additionally, the 
sources of ring-opening enzymes are more diverse, thus promoting the 
ring-opening and metabolism of aromatic organic compounds.
Subsequently, we further conducted the quantitative analysis about 
the contributions of key ring-opening enzymes at the genetic and mi­
crobial species levels for the degradation pathways of aromatic organic 
compounds. The abundance of key functional enzyme genes involved in 
the ring-opening processes was assessed at the KEGG orthology by the 
Reads Per Kilobase of exon model per Million mapped reads (RPKM) 
(Fig. 9(b)). The genes abundance of ring-opening enzymes associated 
from HA to MAHA-2 is noticeably higher. DO, serving as an electron 
acceptor, not only expedited organics degradation but also generated 
more energy to support the metabolism and proliferation of facultative 
microbial species associated with the expression of micro-oxygen ring- 
opening enzymes (Ghosh and Mukherji, 2021; Zhou et al., 2024). This

3.5.2. KEGG pathway annotation of upregulated proteins
The open reading frames annotated in the KEGG database were 
utilized to compare the relative abundance of potential functional genes 
among the reactors. The KEGG pathway enrichment analysis reveals 
that the abundance of 34 distinct functional categories at level 2 exceeds 
0.1 %. In comparison to HA, more than half of these functional cate­
gories exhibit a slight increase in abundance in MAHA-1, with MAHA-2 
demonstrating the highest levels of abundance (Fig. 9(d)). These func­
tional categories are associated with amino acid metabolism, carbohy­
drate metabolism, and energy metabolism. Amino acids are pivotal 
cellular constituents, participating in growth and various metabolic 
processes (Song et al., 2025). In MAHA-2, the abundances of amino acid 
and carbohydrate-related metabolic functions are 8.84 % and 9.24 %, 
respectively, surpassing MAHA-1 (7.86 %, 8.40 %) and HA (7.00 %, 8.31 
%). This indicates the activation of species related to amino acids and 
carbohydrates, thereby enhancing the removal efficiency of organic 
pollutants (e.g., phenols, aromatic compounds, etc.). As depicted in 
Fig. S15, MAHA-2 exhibits relatively higher abundances of genes asso­
ciated with carbon metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis compared 
to MAHA-1 and HA reactors. The above results underscore a significant 
increase in the abundance of functions related to microbial growth and 
the metabolism of organic compounds in MAHA-2, thereby conferring a 
heightened capacity for the organics removal.
3.5.3. Analysis of hydrolase genes related to organics hydrolysis
The hydrolysis process holds significant importance in reducing 
wastewater toxicity and enhancing biodegradability. In this process, 
organic acids were formed when water molecules came into contact with 
organic compounds catalyzed by the relevant hydrolases, resulting in 
the cleavage of chemical bonds (e.g., peptide, ester, and anhydride 
bonds) in the organic molecules (Song et al., 2019). Thus, the analysis of 
hydrolytic genes contributed to understanding the hydrolysis process. 
VFAs molecules bound to water were catalyzed by ester bond hydro­
lases. The cleavage of ester bond released VFAs that promoted the 
growth and metabolism of other microbes. The abundance of ester bond 
hydrolases genes is depicted in Fig. S16. The relative abundances of ester 
bond hydrolases in all reactors are as follows: [EC: 3.1.21.3] hsdS (15, 
924, 22,900, 28,916), hsdR (21,892, 35,688, 40,748), and [EC: 3.1.-.-] 
recJ (15,812, 22,206, 23,416). It is evident that these ester bond hy­
drolases genes exhibit higher abundance in MAHA-2 compared to 
MAHA-1 and HA reactors. The hydrolysis rate of VFAs molecules was 
positively correlated with the abundance of ester bond hydrolases, 
indicating that MAHA-2 possessed a higher abundance of these genes 
encoding ester bond hydrolases, resulting in a stronger ability to hy­
drolyze organic compounds. Furthermore, the hydrolysis of peptide 
bonds was a vital biochemical reaction. Peptide bonds, under the 
catalysis of peptidases, underwent hydrolysis with the generation of 
carboxylic acids and amino groups (Gao et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2021). 
There are multiple types of peptidases, with the abundances of various 
peptidase genes as follows: [EC: 3.4.19.13] ggt (14,514, 22,232, 34, 
476), [EC: 3.4.-.-] K08303 (10,926, 19,532, 21,304), [EC: 3.4.24.-] ftsH, 
hflB (21,408, 23,686, 22,818), pqqL (24,708, 23,164, 20,172), [EC: 
3.4.21.53] lon (24,116, 27,178, 27,538), [EC: 3.4.16.4] mrcA (16,492, 
24,584, 37,930), and [EC: 3.4.11.9] pepP (17,858, 18,552, 20,160). The 
abundances of these peptide bond hydrolases genes are significantly 
higher in MAHA-2 than in MAHA-1 and HA reactors, indicating that the 
microbial community in MAHA-2 possesses a stronger capability to 
hydrolyze peptide bonds, which promotes microbial growth and in­
creases microbial community abundance. Finally, anhydride hydrolases 
catalyzed the hydrolysis of anhydride bonds in organic compounds, 
yielding the corresponding carboxylic acids and alcohols. The abun­
dances of anhydride hydrolases in all reactors are as follows: [EC: 
3.6.3.-] moxR (16,478, 22,864, 23,778), [EC: 3.6.4.-] priA (18,650, 18, 
700, 19,376), [EC: 3.6.4.12] uvrD, pcrA (34,792, 35,094, 33,500), and 
recG (24,468, 28,522, 28,344). These anhydride hydrolases exhibited 
variations in different reactors, because the anaerobic, micro-oxygen, 
and facultative bacteria could participate in anhydride bond hydroly­
sis. Similarly, anhydride hydrolases indirectly enhanced biological ac­
tivity. In summary, the overall abundance of peptide, ester, and 
anhydride bond hydrolases genes in MAHA-2 surpassed that of MAHA-1 
and HA reactors. This suggested that micro-oxygen environment 
contributed to the overall ability of the microbial community to hy­
drolyze organic compounds and produce organic acids, and indirectly 
enhanced the overall biological activity of community.
3.5.4. Biodegradation pathway of phenol
Although qualitative and quantitative relationships between encod­
ing key ring-opening enzymes for aromatic organic compounds and 
functional species have been established through metagenomic analysis, 
a deeper understanding of various functional enzymes in their role and 
metabolic pathways for participating in the biological degradation of 
organic substances is needed. Phenolic substances constituted 60–80 % 
of total organic pollutants in CGW, with phenol being the highest pro­
portion among phenolic organics. Hence, we selected phenol as the 
representative toxic and refractory aromatic organic, and the KEGG 
database was applied for exploring the metabolic pathways of phenol 
and the involved key functional enzymes. As shown in Fig. 10(a), the 
biological degradation pathways of phenol can be divided into micro- 
oxygen pathway A and anaerobic pathway B. In pathway A, the trans­
formation of phenol to catechol is one of the rate-limiting steps during

4. Conclusions
In this study, the cumulative VFAs concentrations in the effluents of 
HA, MAHA-1, and MAHA-2 reactors reached 184.2, 189.9, and 221.8 
mg/L, respectively. TU value of MAHA-2 reactor (~10) after treatment 
was lower than that of HA and MAHA-1 reactors. MAHA-2 reactor 
achieved the lower degree of humification and the reduced concentra­
tion of benzene-ring organics. And MAHA-2 reactor also displays a 
remarkable increase in the concentrations of all functional enzymes and 
ATP. Under this condition, a significant increase in the abundance of 
functions related to microbial growth and the metabolism of organic 
compounds. Especially, higher DO concentration promoted the content 
of protein in EPS. Ultimately, micro-oxygen condition can promote the 
overall activity of microbial community, thus enhancing the removal 
efficiency of pollutants.
